- When sentiment is consistently negative or bearish (e.g., <0.33 or 0.00) and model shows rising trend, reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.  
- After a sharp price spike, model often overcorrects upward — cap forecast growth to 1–2% per day post-spike.  
- If official supply net is negative and sentiment is bearish, model tends to overestimate downside — adjust downward by 2–5% of recent range.  
- When bullish sentiment is low but price is rising, model may overestimate trend — apply downward bias to forecast if recent events are supply-heavy.  
- If sentiment is mixed (0.33–0.67) and price is trending, model often fails to capture mean reversion — add slight downward bias toward 1–3 day horizon.  
- For 30-day forecasts, if recent events are supply-heavy and sentiment is bearish, model tends to overestimate price decline — reduce forecast by 3–7% of recent range.  
- If sentiment is bullish but model forecast is flat or declining, model underestimates upside — increase forecast by 1–3% per day if recent events are demand-heavy.  
- When sentiment is negative and price is falling, model often underestimates depth — adjust forecast downward by 2–5% of recent range.  
- If sentiment is neutral or mixed and model forecast is trending, apply mean reversion bias — forecast should not deviate more than 1.5x recent volatility.  
- For 30-day forecasts, if recent events are auction-heavy and sentiment is bearish, model tends to overestimate price drop — reduce forecast by 3–7% of recent range.
